explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The taunt says, "Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans!" (Habakkuk 2:6). He's stacking up debts like I stack cooling racks, and nobody stacks that high without a wobble.
Taxes aren't in this verse, friend. The taunt says he "…makes himself rich with many loans!" (Habakkuk 2:6). Loans, not taxes, so he's got a whole pile of people waiting to be paid back.

No treasure map here, baker. The taunt says, "Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans!" (Habakkuk 2:6). The verse names loans and never mentions hidden treasure. Hidden treasure is a fun guess, though, and I'd have grabbed a shovel too.

Oh, I wish it worked that way, friend, but it doesn't. The verse asks, "Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey." (Habakkuk 2:7). Forgetting isn't in there. The creditors arise and awaken.

Right, baker, forgetting isn't in this verse. It asks, "Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey." (Habakkuk 2:7). The creditors arise, and the man becomes their prey.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you…" (Habakkuk 2:8). It also names bloodshed and violence, so I think this one is a heavy verse. The plundering he did is the reason given for the plundering that comes to him.

explanations.answer: Because he refused to pay tribute
explanations.explanation: Tribute doesn't come up here, friend. The reason in the verse is, "Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you…" (Habakkuk 2:8). He was the one taking, and now he's the one being taken from.

Mocking is in verse 6, where the nations take up the taunt, but verse 8 gives a different reason. God says, "Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you…" (Habakkuk 2:8). It was the plundering, baker.
That's the word, baker. "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). This is the second woe. The woe falls on the unjust gain behind the house.
Nothing about an inheritance here, friend. The verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). The problem is how the gain was gotten.
Honest isn't the word here, baker. The verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). The word in the text is unjust, and the woe is placed on that man.

You got it, friend. The verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!" (Habakkuk 2:9). I think he figured a nest up high would keep disaster from reaching him. We've all felt safer just by getting farther from the problem.
Neighbors aren't mentioned in this part, baker. The verse says, "…to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!" (Habakkuk 2:9). Disaster is what he hopes to get away from.
I get it, baker, a high spot sounds quiet. But the verse says he places his nest on high "…and escape the hand of disaster!" (Habakkuk 2:9). Disaster is what he's dodging, not noise.

Yes, baker! "For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork." (Habakkuk 2:11). The stones cry out first, and the rafters echo it. Both have a voice in this verse.
Windows are quiet in this verse, friend. God says, "For the stones will cry out from the wall…" (Habakkuk 2:11). The stones are the ones with something to say.

No slamming doors here, baker. The verse says, "For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork." (Habakkuk 2:11). The stones start it, and the rafters join in.

True, baker. "Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!" (Habakkuk 2:12). That's the third woe, after the house woe in verse 9. This one is about a city and a town built with bloodshed and iniquity.
This one is true, friend. God says, "Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!" (Habakkuk 2:12). The house woe came before it, and this city woe is the third.

explanations.answer: The knowledge of the LORD's glory
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. "For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14). After all those woes, this verse hits like the oven door opening on a fresh batch.

explanations.answer: The songs of the freed nations
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, friend, but it's not in the verse. God says, "…the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14). What fills it is the knowledge of the LORD's glory.

explanations.answer: The gold of the fallen cities
explanations.explanation: Gold isn't what fills it, baker. The verse says, "For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14). What fills the earth is the knowledge of the glory of the LORD. Gold isn't named in that verse.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "You will be filled with shame instead of glory." (Habakkuk 2:16). Shame takes the place of glory. It comes in the woe for the one who gives his neighbors drink until they are drunk.
Close in feeling, friend, but not the word. The verse says, "You will be filled with shame instead of glory." (Habakkuk 2:16). Shame takes the place where glory should be.
Nothing about darkness in this verse, baker. God says, "You will be filled with shame instead of glory." (Habakkuk 2:16). Shame is the word, and it takes glory's spot.
That's it, friend. "The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you…" (Habakkuk 2:16). He was passing out the drinks, and now a cup is coming for him from the LORD's hand.
No king in this verse, baker. It says, "The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you…" (Habakkuk 2:16). The cup is in the LORD's hand.
I see why you'd think so, since he poured drinks for his neighbors. But the verse says, "The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you…" (Habakkuk 2:16). The LORD holds this cup, friend.

Correct, baker. The verse says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Lebanon is the place named. The verse also names bloodshed against men, so I think this is a heavy one.
Egypt doesn't show up in this verse, friend. God says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Lebanon is the place named.
Moab isn't named here, baker. The verse says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Lebanon is the one.
True, baker. The verse says, "…the destruction of animals will terrify you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Animals are named right there, next to Lebanon. I think this is a heavy verse, so I'll leave it plain.
It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "…and the destruction of animals will terrify you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Animals are named right there, next to Lebanon.

Right, baker. "For its maker trusts in his own creation; he makes idols that cannot speak." (Habakkuk 2:18). Just before this, the idol is called a teacher of lies. The maker trusts in something that can't say a single word back.
The verse doesn't say anything about breaking, friend. It says, "he makes idols that cannot speak." (Habakkuk 2:18). Speaking is the problem here. The idol can't say a word.
Cost isn't the point here, baker. The verse says, "he makes idols that cannot speak." (Habakkuk 2:18). The maker trusts his own creation, and it can't say a word.

I know it looks alive with all that shine, friend, but it's not. God says, "…it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all." (Habakkuk 2:19). Gold on the outside, no breath inside.

Right, baker. The verse says, "Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all." (Habakkuk 2:19). Sprinkles on a cookie don't make it breathe, and gold doesn't either. The shine is on the outside, and there's no breath in it.
Yes, baker. "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). Right before this, the passage speaks of an idol with no breath in it at all. Now it tells us where the LORD is.
Not quite, friend. The verse says, "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). The temple is the place named.
No city gate in this verse, baker. It says, "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). The temple is the spot.

That's right, friend. The verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). It comes right after "…the LORD is in His holy temple…" All the earth is called to be silent before Him.
I love a good shout, baker, and you know I'm loud. But the verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). Silence is what's asked here.
Gifts aren't mentioned, friend. The verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). Quiet is the whole request.
